claims.text: The balance between configurational entropy and temperature-activated differential atomic diffusion governs the structural and chemical stability of initially homogeneous high-entropy nanoparticles.
Around 473 K, configurational entropy dominates and retains elemental homogeneity.
At temperatures approaching 1923 K, differences in species-specific diffusion kinetics can drive local elemental segregation and phase separation.
The nanoparticles under consideration contain at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and begin as a single-phase solid solution.
Thermal cycling or annealing from 473 K to 1923 K is the proposed intervention.
An inert or controlled atmosphere minimizes extrinsic chemical reactions during thermal treatment.
Sufficiently long thermal holds activate atomic diffusion.
Element-specific diffusion at surfaces and grain boundaries is a structural mediator of thermal instability.
High temperature activates element-specific atomic diffusion.
The constituent metals have different activation energies for atomic migration.
Differences in migration activation energies cause some constituent elements to diffuse faster than others as temperature increases.
Unequal diffusion rates lead to localized elemental segregation or phase separation.
The nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure at lower temperatures.
Near 1923 K, elemental segregation or secondary phases will emerge relative to the initial homogeneous state.
High-temperature segregation or secondary phases will occur especially at surfaces or interfaces.
The mechanism is expected to prevail when external reactive influences are minimized and thermal energy is sufficient to activate differential diffusion.
Absence of detectable segregation, phase separation, or deviation from the homogeneous baseline near 1923 K despite diffusion-activating conditions would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
